All other moves let the white king go straight to f5 or e5, onto a key square of the pawn on e3. Remember: with the opposition, what counts is who is to move. The same position can be a draw or lost.

texte.40ca597b2566: {z1} The kings then stand on the f-file with three squares between them, and White is to move: Black has the distant opposition. The key squares of the pawn on e2 are d4, e4 and f4. If the white king approaches, Black switches to the direct opposition: {z2} or {z3}, and the white king reaches no key square. The obvious {z4} loses, since White then takes the opposition with {z5}. {z6} loses too, for example after {z7}, and so do all other moves. Remember: as the kings approach, the distant opposition turns into the direct opposition. Both times it is decisive that the other side is to move.
texte.0b2108ec0233: After 1... Kf6! the kings stand on the f-file three squares apart, and White is to move: distant opposition. If the white king comes closer, 2... Ke5 or 2... Kf5 turns it into the direct opposition, and d4, e4 and f4 stay blocked.

texte.0ae182cffb2b: Yes, but only with precise play: {z1} The key squares of the pawn on d4 are c6, d6 and e6. After {z2}, {z3} takes the opposition, and Black has to give one of them up: {z4} or {z5}. On {z6}, {z7} goes there at once; on {z8}, {z9}. The obvious move {z10}, by contrast, throws away the win, because then Black has the opposition with {z11}. Without the rook trade White does not win in this position. texte.2543a7813c0a: Yes, but only with {z1}: after the double step the square reaches from a4 to e8, and the king on g5 can no longer reach it. After {z2}, on the other hand, the king catches the pawn. (If the black king stood on f5, the position would be a draw even after {z3}.) Remember: if the pawn stands on its starting square, you draw the square one rank further forward.
texte.abd304be9317: After the double step 1. a4! the square reaches from a4 to e8, and the king on g5 can no longer get into it. After 1. a3? it catches the pawn; if the pawn stands on its starting square, you draw the square one rank further forward.
texte.f9236667f34f: Both pawns still need two moves to promote. Does White win the race? Answer the four questions about the pawn race.
texte.91dac1448a5a: Yes: {z1}. White promotes first (question 1), and with check (question 2), since the king on c3 stands on the long diagonal. Black has to move the king and does not get to promote. On {z2} or {z3}, the queen places itself on the promotion square with {z4} (question 3), and the white king picks up the pawn. After {z5} this is the only winning move. The fourth question does not arise, because Black gets no queen. If Black moves the king off the diagonal beforehand, for example with {z6}, Black is a tempo short: {z7}. The toughest defense is {z8}: after {z9} White needs a queen check, such as {z10}, so that the pawn does not get to a2. Any first move other than {z11} allows a draw. Remember: before a pawn race, check whether a king stands on a file, rank or diagonal that the new queen controls.
texte.18905a378d53: White promotes first and with check, because the king on c3 stands on the long diagonal; then the queen places itself in front of the a-pawn with Qa1. Before every pawn race, check whether a king stands on a line of the new queen.
texte.00e65d7b9c82: White is a pawn up, and two moves suggest themselves: {z1} and {z2}. Which one wins, and why does the other one fail?
texte.cb7cfc1373ec: {z1} wins, {z2} throws away the win: after {z3} White does have a passed pawn, but the king stands behind it instead of in front of it. It no longer reaches the key squares of the pawn on f5 (e6, f6, g6 and e7, f7, g7): draw. After {z4} the pawn on g6 is fixed, and {z5} stays in reserve as a lever. First the king goes to work, and with the opposition: {z6} is met by {z7}, {z8} by {z9}, {z10} by the diagonal opposition {z11}. Each time the black king has to give way, and the white king penetrates via d6 or f6 and wins the pawn on g6. On {z12}, {z13} wins at once, since g6 is a key square of the pawn on g5. Remember: create the passed pawn only when your king then reaches a key square.
texte.ab552e88fd0a: Passed pawn only with the king in front
texte.193e10f31007: 1. g5! fixes the pawn on g6, keeps f5 in reserve as a lever, and the white king penetrates with the opposition. After 1. f5+? gxf5+ 2. gxf5+ the king stands behind its passed pawn and reaches no key square: draw.
texte.49f181926d2b: White is a pawn up. Describe the plan with which White wins, and name a first move.
texte.de86cd021dbe: The h-pawn is an outside passed pawn, which White pushes until the black king has to stop it. Then the white king collects the black queenside pawns: for example {z1}, and the white king captures both black pawns before the black king is back. If the king instead runs to the white pawns with {z2}, it stands outside the square, and the h-pawn becomes a queen. Quiet moves such as {z3} also win; the plan stays the same. Remember: the outside passed pawn ties down the king, and your king harvests on the other wing.
texte.45f82787286d: White pushes the h-pawn until the black king has to stop it, and meanwhile collects the queenside pawns with the king. The outside passed pawn ties down the king, and your own king harvests on the other wing.
texte.c268343212a4: Two king moves give stalemate. Which are they, and how does White win instead?
texte.046b1cdb2a06: {z1} and {z2} give stalemate, since the king on a8 has no square and the pawn on b7 is blocked. The pawn sacrifice {z3} wins: after {z4} Black only has the pawn move {z5}, and {z6} is mate. If Black does not capture, {z7} decides. The position arises from {v1} when the black king retreats to the 8th rank after the triangle and the white king penetrates via d6 and e7 to d7. Remember: before you take the king's last square away, check whether your opponent still has a pawn move.
texte.900ef5bdded5: 1. Kc7?? and 1. Kc8?? give stalemate. The sacrifice 1. c6! leaves Black a pawn move: after 1... bxc6 2. Kc7 c5 3. b7+ White soon gives mate; after 1... Kb8 2. c7+ Ka8 3. c8=Q#.
texte.bcf00fc91ae1: White has two pawn moves to choose from: {z1} and {z2}. Which one wins, and why does the other one lose?
texte.0436e3e47c68: {z1} wins. As in {v1}, whoever has to move the king loses. After {z2} the a-pawns are blocked: Black has to move the king and loses the pawn on f5. On {z3}, {z4} turns the picture around: now White has no pawn move left, has to move the king and loses the pawn on f4 and the game, since the double step used up both spare tempi at once. Remember: count the pawn moves of both sides before you spend one of them.
texte.50d4d0b07ac3: 1. a3! keeps a pawn move in reserve: after 1... a5 2. a4 Black has to move the king and loses f5. The double step 1. a4? uses up both tempi at once, and after 1... a5! White has to give way.
